items.followUp: Explain the population level and ecosystem level of biological organization.

rubric.why: The organism level refers to one individual organism.
rubric.description: Identifies the organism as an individual.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an organism is an individual.

rubric.why: An organism is a living thing.
rubric.description: States that an organism is a living thing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing an organism as a living thing.

rubric.why: A community consists of populations belonging to different species.
rubric.description: Identifies the populations and species that make up a community.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both populations and different species are stated.

rubric.why: The populations in a community live in the same area or habitat.
rubric.description: States where the populations of a community live.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they live in the same area or habitat.

rubric.why: The populations in a community interact with one another.
rubric.description: States that community members interact.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning interaction among the populations or species.

modelAnswer: Organism level: An organism is an individual living thing, such as a plant or an animal.
Community level: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus, whereas eukaryotic cells have one.
rubric.description: Compares the presence of a membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the nucleus in both cell types.

rubric.why: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, while eukaryotes contain them.
rubric.description: Compares membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the organelles in both cell types.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular, whereas eukaryotic DNA forms linear chromosomes associated with proteins.
rubric.description: Compares the genetic material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting prokaryotic DNA with eukaryotic linear chromosomes.

rubric.why: Bacteria are prokaryotes, whereas plant, animal, and fungal cells are eukaryotic.
rubric.description: Gives suitable examples of both cell types.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying bacteria as prokaryotic and a plant, animal, or fungal cell as eukaryotic.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles.
Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular; eukaryotic DNA forms linear chromosomes associated with proteins.
Bacteria are prokaryotes, whereas plant, animal, and fungal cells are eukaryotic.

items.followUp: Describe how fermentation is used in bread-making and in the production of yoghurt.

rubric.why: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose; yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: Defines fermentation and gives its products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing anaerobic glucose breakdown and naming ethanol and carbon dioxide as products.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide produced by yeast makes bread dough rise.
rubric.description: Explains the role of fermentation in bread-making.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking carbon dioxide production with dough rising.

rubric.why: Yeast fermentation is used to produce alcoholic drinks.
rubric.description: States another use of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast fermentation in alcoholic-drink production.

rubric.why: Lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars to produce lactic acid in yoghurt and some cheeses.
rubric.description: Explains fermentation in dairy-food production.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking lactic acid bacteria and lactic acid production with yoghurt, yogurt, or cheese.

modelAnswer: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose; yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
In bread-making, carbon dioxide produced by yeast makes the dough rise.
Yeast fermentation is also used to produce alcoholic drinks such as beer and wine.
Lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars to make yoghurt and some cheeses.

items.followUp: Explain how guard cells cause stomata to open and close.

rubric.why: In light, photosynthesis in guard cells increases the concentration of their cell sap.
rubric.description: Explains the change in guard cells in light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking light and photosynthesis with increased cell-sap concentration.

rubric.why: Water enters guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and the stomata open.
rubric.description: Explains stomatal opening.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water entry, turgidity, and opening.

rubric.why: In darkness, sugar in guard cells is converted to starch, lowering the concentration of their cell sap.
rubric.description: Explains the change in guard cells in darkness.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking darkness and conversion of sugar to starch with reduced cell-sap concentration.

rubric.why: Water leaves guard cells by osmosis; they become flaccid and the stomata close.
rubric.description: Explains stomatal closing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water loss, flaccidity, and closing.

modelAnswer: In light, photosynthesis in guard cells increases the concentration of their cell sap.
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and the stomata open.
In darkness, sugar in guard cells is converted to starch, lowering the concentration of their cell sap.
Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis; they become flaccid and the stomata close.

items.followUp: Name one contribution made by Jabir bin Hayan to science.

rubric.why: Jabir bin Hayan is known as the father of chemistry.
rubric.description: Gives his famous title.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying him as the father of chemistry.

rubric.why: He contributed to the development of experimental methods in chemistry.
rubric.description: States his contribution to chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning his contribution to experimental methods in chemistry.

modelAnswer: Jabir bin Hayan was a famous Muslim scientist known as the father of chemistry.
He contributed to the development of experimental methods in chemistry.

items.followUp: Give one reason why measurements made with instruments are useful in biology.

rubric.why: Quantitative observations express results as numerical measurements.
rubric.description: States what quantitative observations provide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that quantitative observations use numerical measurements.

rubric.why: Numerical measurements are more precise and objective, allowing results to be compared more reliably than descriptive observations.
rubric.description: Explains why quantitative observations are more accurate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating a valid advantage such as greater precision, objectivity, or reliable comparison.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations give results as numerical measurements.
These measurements are more precise and objective than descriptions, so they can be compared more reliably.

items.followUp: What is a variable in an experiment, and why should only one variable be changed at a time?

rubric.why: A control provides a standard or comparison for judging experimental results.
rubric.description: Defines the purpose of a control.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a control provides a standard or comparison.

rubric.why: In a controlled experiment, conditions are kept the same except for the variable being tested.
rubric.description: Explains how a control helps make a fair comparison.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that conditions remain the same apart from the variable being tested.

modelAnswer: A control is the standard or comparison used to judge the results of an experiment.
All conditions are kept the same except for the one variable being tested.
